opener.heading: Week 9: My Body & Senses 🖐️
about: Seven days on the outside and the inside of Azlyn. She gets drawn round at life size, sorts ten textures from rough to soft, pulls a face at a lemon, prints her hands and feet down the hall, holds six faces in a mirror while you photograph them, tests three paper ear trumpets and names six smells without being told what is in the pots. Each day hands her one sense and something solid to measure it against.

February ends on Sunday and March starts on Monday, so the March handprint goes on the card first thing on Day 60, third of twelve, while her hands are still clean. That card and the fingerprint card are what you keep. The life-size outline rolls up under a bed, the dough family gets photographed and squashed back into a lump, and the touch line lasts until somebody needs the cardboard.
azlyn: Body parts by name. Ankle, wrist, elbow, ear, learned while your pencil is touching each one.
Sorting on a scale she invents. Ten textures laid out from rough to soft, and her order is the one that stands.
Four tastes and a word for each. Sweet, salty, sour and bitter, one saucer at a time, with yogurt to clear her mouth between them.
Whole-arm work. Drawing at floor scale, squeezing lemons, kneading dough and pressing it flat.
Fair testing. Three paper ear trumpets, one sound, one distance, one thing changed at a time.
you: Big movements come before small ones
Repetitive, contained tasks are surprisingly regulating
Three dimensions are harder than two, and worth the time
Testing before committing is a habit worth encouraging
She tells you what it is once nobody has asked
shopping: Cardboard boxes to flatten, or a roll of butcher paper, longer than Azlyn lying down
Plain paper, a stack, and thin card, 4 sheets
Fat crayons, plus a box of ordinary ones
A pencil, a fine pen and a permanent marker
A fabric scrap, a ribbon, an emery board, a bottle cap, a piece of corrugated card and a leaf off the path
A dishpan, 2 smaller bowls and 1 shallow bowl
A pitcher, 3 cups, 2 spoons and a whisk
Washable non-toxic poster paint in red, yellow, white and brown
A wide soft brush, plus a dry one for Kreston
Jam, for a second sweet taste
Salt, 500 g (a cup of it goes into the playdough)
Ground coffee, ground cinnamon and a cinnamon stick
A dried herb, a sliver of soap and a drop of vanilla
A table knife, a fork and a small sieve
A lemon squeezer, or a second fork instead
Yogurt cups or paper cups, 8, cleaned out
Wooden spoons, 2, and a metal one
A saucepan for banging and a small one for the stovetop
A small rigid pot with a lid, for Kreston's own lump of dough
Your phone, charged, for the six faces, the sour face and the family photo
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 8 months this week. He crawls or shuffles, bangs two things together for the noise of it, and has arrived at being wary of new faces. He turns 9 months on Friday the 5th, the first day of next week.

days.title: Head to Toe
days.prepTonight: Flatten every box you have, or unroll butcher paper, tape the pieces into one sheet longer than Azlyn, and leave it rolled by the hall door.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The Biggest Paper in the House

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Naming the Parts in the Bath

opening.title: The Biggest Paper in the House
opening.need: the taped sheet or flattened boxes · 1 roll masking tape · fat crayons.
steps: Unroll the whole thing down the hall and let her walk the length of it in socks.
Have her lie down on it in three different shapes while you tape the corners to the floor. Arms out, arms in, one leg up.
Ask which shape she wants to keep. That is the pose she holds at 9:15, so let her practice while you count to twenty.

main.title: The Life-Size Azlyn
materials: Flattened cardboard boxes or a roll of butcher paper, enough to cover her lying down
Fat crayons, one for each hand
steps: She lies down in the pose she chose. Draw round her with the pencil, feet first, naming as you go: ankle, knee, hip, elbow, wrist, ear. Keep the pencil touching her so she can feel where you are.
Get her up and let her look. She will not know it for herself at first, and standing beside something her own size is the reason for all that paper.
Go over the pencil line with the marker together, your hand starting each stretch and hers finishing it.
Give her the mirror and let her study her own face before she draws it in. Do not name the parts for her. She puts in what she sees, and one eye will be bigger.
Hand her a fat crayon for each hand. The clothes get filled in standing up and leaning over, whole arm, not sitting down with her wrist on the floor.
Write her name and the date across the top, then stand it against a wall where she walks past it.
main.tip: Draw round her in one continuous line, including the bit that goes wrong under her armpit. Lifting the pencil to tidy the shape turns her outline into your drawing.

outside.title: Standing Next to Things
paras: She has spent the morning beside a drawing of herself, so take her out and stand her against the street. Back to the lamp post, back to the mailbox, one hand flat on a car wheel, both feet on the bottom step of a porch. Taller or shorter, said out loud each time. Find one thing on the whole walk that comes out the same height as she does.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months and bangs two things together with great pleasure and no purpose beyond the noise. Lay him at the far end of the paper with two wooden spoons: crackle underneath, racket on top. Draw round one of his feet on a corner of the sheet while he is down there. He will kick the pencil away twice before you get it.

second.title: Inside the Outline
second.intro: She fills in the parts of herself she has never seen.
steps: Ask her where her heart is and let her put a flat hand on the spot she picks. Take the answer as it comes.
Tear a heart out of the red paper rather than cutting one. Torn edges hand her the whole job and it can come out lopsided.
Stick it on the outline where she said. Then hold the cardboard tube to her own chest and let her listen until she finds the beat, and let her hear yours after.
Cut long strips of pink paper for bones while she watches, and let her lay them down the arms and legs. Have her squeeze her own forearm first to meet the hard line inside it.
Add a tummy, one big oval stuck low down, and tell her what goes in and how long the trip takes.
Stand her up and count twenty jumps out loud, then the tube back on her chest the second she stops.
Ask her what changed. Write her answer on the outline beside the heart, word for word.
second.tip: Roll the outline up tonight instead of throwing it out. She goes back to it at 4:15, and it stores flat under a bed.

alternatives: Draw round her hands and feet only, on ordinary paper.
Draw round a teddy and let her fill that in instead.
Lie down on the floor and let her draw round you.
outAgain: Meet a friend at the park, and take the outline along to show somebody
The park on your own, for the swings and the cold
A friend's house, kettle on, both children on the floor
The long way home, counting who you pass who is taller than her

aroundWorld.title: Hello Everywhere 👋
paras: Hellos are made with the body, and every place picks a different part of it. In Japan people bow, and the deeper bow carries the more respect. Māori in New Zealand greet with the hongi, pressing noses and foreheads together. In much of France it is kisses on the cheek, and the number changes from town to town.
aroundWorld.tryIt: In many countries a guest gets food before conversation. Set a small plate of bread or dates up on the side and let Azlyn hand it to whoever comes in today.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: In the hongi, two people share one breath.

days.krestonPM: At 8 months he has arrived at being wary of new faces, so keep him on you at the park instead of passed round. He will study your friend from your shoulder before he decides. Back home, lie him on his back and let Azlyn hold the tube over his chest. He grabs it, which counts as taking part.

insight.headline: Big movements come before small ones.
paras: Azlyn's control grows from the middle of her body outward: shoulder before elbow, elbow before wrist, wrist before fingers. Sweeping a crayon across paper the size of herself builds the shoulder and trunk strength that a pencil grip later sits on top of. Occupational therapists ask for floor-scale and vertical work for that reason, and the bigger the surface, the more of her arm has to join in. A sheet of letter paper on a table asks her fingers for control her shoulder has not earned yet. Give her the floor, the wall and the driveway this year and the small stuff turns up on its own.

days.safety: Scissors stay with you and go back out of reach between cuts. Torn scraps, tape and the glue stick come off the floor the moment you stop watching Kreston. Bread and dates are a choking hazard at 8 months, so that plate stays up on the side, not down by the door where he travels.

days.title: The Feel of Things
days.prepTonight: Cut a meter-long strip from the side of a box and leave it on the table with the packing tape, and put two old towels by the sink.

opening.title: Ten Things That Feel Different
opening.need: 1 paper bag · the run of the house · her hands.
steps: Hand her the bag and walk her round the rooms. She collects ten things that feel different, one per room if she stalls.
Keep your hands out of the choosing. If she takes the emery board and leaves the ribbon in the drawer, the ribbon stays in the drawer.
Sit on the floor and lay all ten in a line. Ask which is the roughest, leave that one at the end of the row, and go and have breakfast.

main.title: The Touch Line
materials: 1 long strip of cardboard, about a meter
Ten household textures: foil, cotton balls, corrugated card, fabric scrap, ribbon, an emery board, a bottle cap, a leaf, a strip of tape sticky side up, a sponge
steps: Lay the strip on the floor and tape the roughest thing she picked at one end. That end is fixed, and everything else gets placed against it.
Work along the strip. Each new thing has to feel softer than the one before, and she decides. Tape across the middle of each so the edges stay free to touch.
Let her change her mind. Peel the fabric off and move it two places down if she says so. The arguing is the sorting.
Put the strip of tape sticky side up somewhere in the middle. It sits outside her scale, and she will say so.
Write her word for each one underneath in marker. Scratchy, fluffy, bumpy, sharpy, whatever comes out of her.
Shut her eyes, set her finger on the rough end and let her run it down the line. She calls out where she thinks she has got to, then opens her eyes and checks.
main.tip: Do not fix her order. Softness is a scale she is inventing this morning, and hers holds together even where yours would run another way.

outside.title: Bare Hands on Cold Things
paras: Gloves off for a minute at a time. Flat palm on a car roof, a metal gate, a brick wall, a railing in the sun and the same railing in the shade. Metal pulls heat out of her hand faster than brick, so the gate feels colder than the wall at the same temperature and she will say so. Gloves back on the moment she says cold.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months and traveling now, so the floor belongs to him. Tape a palm-sized square of foil, fabric, corrugated card and sponge onto a tray and set it in his path. He crawls up, plants a hand on the foil and stops dead. Keep every square bigger than his mouth.

second.title: The Warm Water Table
second.intro: Two bowls on old towels on the kitchen floor, and nothing in the next ninety minutes has to be finished.
steps: Fill the big bowl with warm water, wrist-tested, and the small one with cold. Set them a hand's width apart on the towels.
Both hands into the warm bowl, count to ten together, then both hands into the cold and count again. Ask her which hand knows the difference.
Put out the pitcher, cups, spoons, sponges and whisk, then sit down where she can see you and stop giving instructions.
She will pour one bowl into the other within four minutes. Let the two temperatures become one and let her hands find out.
Drop two drops of coloring into the cold bowl as interest dips. That buys you the whole second half.
Hand her a sponge to soak and squeeze out over the big bowl. Heavy work for her hands, and she stays with it longest of all.
Tip both bowls into the sink yourself the moment she walks away.
second.tip: Change her top, not the plan. A wet shirt ends the afternoon at one thirty, and a dry one buys you another twenty minutes.

alternatives: One bowl, warm water, one cup, nothing else.
Ice cubes dropped into warm water, no goal beyond watching.
Feet in the bowl instead of hands.
outAgain: The fire station, or a field with a tractor in it, whichever is nearer
A construction site fence, for diggers doing something loud
The pet store, for warm fur and cold glass
The park, for cold metal, wet rope and a slide that stings
days.krestonPM: He goes in the sling or the highchair while the bowls are on the floor, and out of the room the second you cannot watch both children. Once the water is gone, hand him a dry bowl, a wooden spoon and a metal one. Banging two things together is his month's work, and the metal spoon wins.

insight.headline: Repetitive, contained tasks are surprisingly regulating.
paras: Azlyn will pour the same pitcher into the same bowl thirty times, and you will start wondering when she plans to do something with it. The repetition is the activity. A task with a clear edge round it, one bowl, one pitcher, one action, hands her a small world she controls on a day when adults decide most of the rest. The feedback never changes, so her body stops bracing for surprises and settles. Montessori classrooms are built on this. Set it out, sit down, say nothing, and let it run well past the point where you have had enough of it.

days.safety: Standing water and a newly crawling 8-month-old. Kreston can drown in the depth of a dishpan in the time it takes to answer the door. Tip it out the moment she is finished, and never leave the room with it full. The touch line lies on the floor with a bottle cap, cotton balls and a leaf taped along it, all small enough to choke Kreston at 8 months, so keep the strip out of his crawling path, press every piece of tape down hard, and lift the whole thing onto the table the moment she leaves it.

days.title: Four Tastes
days.prepTonight: Put a lemon, crackers, an apple, the cocoa and the yogurt on the counter with four saucers and four teaspoons, and check you have three more lemons for the afternoon.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: What the Birds Left on the Stems

opening.title: Cutting the Tasting Plate
opening.need: 1 lemon · 1 apple · plain crackers · 1 table knife · 4 small saucers.
steps: Sit her at the table and let her hold the whole lemon in both hands, smell the skin and roll it before anything gets cut.
You cut the lemon into thin wedges. She cuts the apple beside you with a table knife on a board, slow and under your hand.
She loads one saucer per taste and decides where each saucer sits on the table. Nobody tastes a thing before 9:15, and telling her that is most of the hour.

main.title: The Sour Face Test
materials: Plain crackers and a pinch of salt
Apple slices or a little jam
Plain unsweetened cocoa, a dab on a teaspoon, for bitter
Plain yogurt to reset her mouth between tastes
steps: Line the four saucers up in front of her: apple, cracker with salt, lemon, and the dab of cocoa. Yogurt goes in the middle as the reset.
Start with the sweet one so she trusts the game. Photograph her face while she is tasting, not after.
Ask for a word before you offer one of your own. Write her word on the paper under a rough drawing of that saucer.
Lemon next. Have the camera up before it reaches her mouth, because the face lasts about a second and a half.
Salt, then cocoa last. A spoon of yogurt between each one clears her mouth and gives her something to look forward to.
Read the four words back in order and let her choose which taste she wants again. Give her that one.
main.tip: Let her spit the cocoa out. Bitter keeps small children away from what would harm them, and her body doing its job is worth the mess.

outside.title: What the Birds Left on the Stems
paras: The last morning of February, and the berries are down to whatever nobody wanted. Walk a hedge, a fence line or a front yard and sort the stems into two kinds: stripped bare, or still loaded. Sumac heads, rose hips, crabapples, holly, the dry seed heads on last year's coneflowers. Ask her which ones the birds went for first. Nothing comes off the stem and nothing goes near a mouth.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months and gets none of the four saucers, but he can sit in the highchair through the whole thing with a strip of soft apple or a spoon of plain yogurt. Watch his face when the yogurt lands. He is wary of new things this month and checks yours first, so let him see you eat before he commits.

second.title: Fixing the Lemonade
second.intro: Three lemons, a pitcher and a bag of sugar. She is in charge of how it tastes and you are the one doing what she says.
steps: Halve the lemons and let her squeeze them. A fork stabbed into the cut half and twisted works as well as a squeezer and takes more effort out of her arms.
Pour the juice through the sieve into the pitcher. Let her taste it neat, one teaspoon. The face from this morning comes back.
Add sugar a spoon at a time. She stirs, she tastes with a clean spoon, she says more or stop.

She will overshoot and make it too sweet to drink. Say nothing, hand her the water and let her add a splash at a time, tasting after each one, until she works out she can go too far in both directions.
She calls it finished. That is the recipe, and nobody adjusts it after she has said so.
She pours a cup for every person in the house and carries them round herself.
second.tip: Give her a clean teaspoon for each taste and keep them in a row. Tasting from the stirring spoon is how she ends up drinking the whole pitcher.

alternatives: Squeeze one lemon into a glass of water and stop there.
Sweeten plain yogurt to her order instead.
Set up a doorstep lemonade stand for the family only.
outAgain: The scooter or the balance bike, on the flattest path you know
Feeding the ducks with this morning's crusts
A playground you drive past and never stop at
The yard or the front step, with the lemonade pitcher
days.krestonPM: At 8 months he goes in the stroller while she scoots, and the wheels beside him are the entertainment. Stop somewhere flat and put him down on a rug with a plastic pitcher and a wooden spoon. He fills, tips, bangs and starts again. Keep the squeezed lemon halves and every seed away from him.

insight.headline: The gasp is the learning.
paras: The face Azlyn pulls when the lemon lands is her brain filing something away. She predicted one thing, got another, and that mismatch is what makes the memory stick. Researchers working with babies and toddlers find that a child explores an object for longer, and remembers more about it, after it has done something she did not expect. Surprise flags the moment as worth keeping. You cannot manufacture it by explaining first, which is the argument for handing her the lemon before you say the word sour. Her face doing that beats her repeating the word back to you at dinnertime.

days.safety: Kreston is 8 months and gets none of this. No honey before one year, no salt, no lemonade. Cut anything he does get into strips rather than rounds, stay at his eye level while he eats, and keep grapes, whole crackers and lemon rind off the floor where he now travels.

days.title: Hands and Feet
days.prepTonight: Tape paper or flattened boxes end to end down the hall floor, and check you have 2 cups of flour and a cup of salt, because tomorrow's playdough gets made tonight.

opening.title: Mixing Her Own Color
opening.need: red, yellow, white and brown poster paint · 4 saucers · 1 wide soft brush.
steps: Put a blob of red, white and brown on three saucers and leave the fourth empty.
She mixes her own skin color in the empty saucer. She adds, you stir, she holds the back of her hand next to it and checks.
Keep going until she says it matches. Nobody else gets a vote, and the color she lands on is the one you use for the next two hours.

main.title: Ten Fingers, Ten Toes
materials: Washable non-toxic poster paint in red, yellow, white and brown
A long strip of paper or flattened boxes taped end to end
1 sheet of thick card for the March handprint
1 bowl of warm soapy water and 2 old towels, set up before you start
steps: Water bowl and towels at the far end of the paper before a drop of paint comes out of the tub.
Do the March handprint first, on the thick card, while her hands are clean. Brush the paint on, press flat, count to three, lift straight up. Write March and 3 beside it. Third of twelve.
Paint one palm and let her print her way down the paper roll however she likes. Some will smear.
Sit her on a chair at the end of the roll and paint the soles of her feet with the brush. She will laugh and snatch her foot back, and the arch is the worst of it.
Hold both her hands and walk her the length of the paper. Slow steps. Wet paper slides on a hard floor, so keep hold the whole way.
Straight into the warm water, feet first, before she stands anywhere else.
main.tip: Paint her, do not dip her. A loaded brush leaves a thin even layer and gives you a print with the lines in it. A saucer gives you a blob.

outside.title: Boot Prints in the Mud
paras: March mud is the best mud of the year, wet through and no longer frozen. Go hunting in it for prints somebody else left: a bird, a dog, a tire, the ridged sole of a boot. Work out together who came past and which way they went. The soft ones fill with water while you watch, which she will report to you at length.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months and gets one foot printed on the card beside Azlyn's hand. Sit him on your lap facing away, washcloth open on your knee, brush the sole and press the card up to the foot rather than the foot down to the card. Then he stays out of the hall, because a crawling baby and a painted floor make a bad afternoon.

second.title: Everybody's Fingerprints
second.intro: One saucer, one fingertip each, and every person in the house on a single sheet of card.
materials: 1 magnifying glass, or your phone camera zoomed in
1 wet washcloth in a shallow bowl
steps: Press one finger of each person into the paint and onto the card, in a row, and write the name under each print in pen.
Do Kreston's while he is calm, with the washcloth already in your other hand.
Hand her the magnifying glass and hold the flashlight at a low angle across the card, so the loops throw shadows and lift off the paper.
Compare two prints at a time and ask her to find one difference. Yours against hers is the easiest pair to start on.
Press a clean finger onto a window and shine the flashlight sideways at it, so she meets the print she leaves without any paint at all.
Write the date on the card and store it with this morning's handprint card.
second.tip: Tell her once that nobody in the world has her pattern, including Kreston, then stop talking and let her sit with it.

alternatives: Thumbprints only, turned into caterpillars with a pen.
Hunt for her own prints on the fridge door with the flashlight.
Paint one big handprint each and hang them side by side.
outAgain: The riverside path, to see how high the water is running after the rain
The neighborhood park, boots on and nobody there
A puddle circuit with no destination
The mailbox, and let her push the letter in
days.krestonPM: At 8 months the stroller is fine for the path, but give him ten minutes out of it on a blanket somewhere flat. He crawls to the edge, meets grass with his palm and stops to think about it. Let him meet cold ground on purpose while you sit there, then back in the stroller before his hands cool.

insight.headline: Process art versus product art.
paras: Azlyn wanted the cold paint on her palm, the squelch under her heel and the walking. The sheet of paper at the end is a by-product of ninety seconds she enjoyed. Three-year-olds meet almost every material this way, and a child asked to produce something recognizable spends the session watching your face to find out whether it counts. You did keep one thing today, the March handprint, and a keepsake is a fair reason to steer her hands for two minutes. Hang the rest of the roll in the hall for a week, then let it go, and tell her that is the plan.

days.safety: A painted foot on a hard floor slides out from under her. Keep the printing to one room, towels down at both ends, and wipe her soles before she steps off the paper. Washable non-toxic paint only, and keep the saucers off the floor while Kreston is crawling.

days.title: Making a Face
days.prepTonight: Make the playdough while the kettle boils: 2 cups flour, 1 cup salt, 1 tbsp oil, 1 cup water, kneaded warm, and leave it bagged on the counter with the hand mirror.

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Dough Family in a Tub

opening.title: Two Colors of Dough
opening.need: the dough · food coloring · 2 bowls · a floured board.
steps: Split the dough in half and put a few drops of color into the middle of each lump. She pushes the color in with her thumbs.
Knead until the streaks disappear. It takes longer than she expects, which is the reason it sits at 8:00 and not at 9:15.
Ask who she plans to build this afternoon. Let her say it out loud, then leave her the morning to change her mind, because she will.

main.title: Six Faces in the Mirror
materials: 1 hand mirror, propped so she can see her whole face without holding it
A chair she can kneel up on at the table
steps: Prop the mirror where the light is good and kneel her up at the table beside it.
Do the first face yourself. Eyebrows up, mouth open, and hold it while she looks at you and then at herself doing it back.
Work through six: surprised, cross, sleepy, sad, silly, and one she invents and names. She holds each one while you photograph it.
Ask what her face is doing each time, part by part. Eyebrows, eyes, mouth. Write her words on a sheet under a rough drawing of that face.
Lay the six photographs out on the phone and let her match each one to the words you wrote. Two of them will surprise her.
Tape the six sheets up at her height where she walks past them, in the order she picks.
main.tip: Photograph her while the face is still on. A three-year-old asked to hold an expression drops it inside two seconds, so shoot first and talk afterwards.

outside.title: Faces on the Ground
paras: Take a bag and collect face parts off the ground: two matching stones for eyes, a stick for a mouth, a curl of bark for a nose, moss or dead grass for hair. Build the face on a flat bit of sidewalk or on a tree stump and leave it there for whoever comes next. Photograph it and check tomorrow whether it survived.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months and faces are his subject this month. Hold the mirror in front of him and watch him reach for the baby in it, then hide behind your hands and come back. Wariness and delight arrive in the same ten seconds. Give him a lump of dough shut in a small rigid pot, lid taped on hard, while Azlyn works.

second.title: A Family That Stands Up
second.intro: Everyone in the house gets made out of dough, and every one of them has to stand on the tray without falling over.
materials: 1 flat tray as the standing ground
2 cardboard tubes cut short, for anyone who needs a stand
A photo of the family on your phone
A ruler or a strip of card for comparing heights
steps: Prop your phone up with the family photo on it where she can see it while she works.
Start with the smallest. Kreston is a body, a head and no legs worth speaking of, so he stands up on the first try.
Azlyn next. She rolls two legs and tests them on the tray before the head goes on top.
One of them will topple. Ask her what would fix it and wait. Thicker legs, bigger feet or a tube behind the back are all fair answers, and she picks.
Build the tall ones last. They fall over most, and by then she has three collapses behind her to work from.
Stand the whole family on the tray in height order, measure them against the ruler, and photograph the row beside the real family photo so she can tell you who is who.
second.tip: Fat legs and big feet hold a dough person up, and she gets there by watching three of them fall. Do not fix the first one for her.

alternatives: Flat dough people lying on the tray, no standing required.
Make the family out of clothespins and scrap fabric instead.
Build only Kreston, twenty times, because that is where she is.
outAgain: Swimming, and she gets herself changed this year
The indoor play center if the session is booked out
The library, a day early
A long bath at home and an early dinner, if the morning ran hot
days.krestonPM: At 8 months the changing room is full of strangers, so keep him facing you until you are both in the water. He sits supported in your hands and slaps the surface with two flat palms, and twenty minutes of that will do him. Get him out and dressed before he cools.

insight.headline: Three dimensions are harder than two, and worth the time.
paras: Drawing a person on paper asks Azlyn to flatten something she has only ever met as a solid. Dough lets her keep it solid, and a body that has to stand up on the tray sets her a problem no crayon can. She holds the shape in her head, turns it over, checks it against the photograph and adjusts. Spatial thinking of that sort predicts later math ability, on top of what counting practice gives her, and it responds to this kind of work: hands on material, objects turned round, decisions about how a thing sits. Twenty minutes of dough beats twenty worksheets, and she stays with it longer.

days.safety: Salt dough is dangerous swallowed, and at 8 months Kreston puts everything in his mouth and can now reach the table leg. Give him his own pot of dough with the lid taped on hard, and nothing loose. The table knife and the cut tubes go back up out of reach the moment the family is standing. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: What Ears Are For
days.prepTonight: Put four sheets of paper, the masking tape and two rubber bands on the table, and wind off five meters of string onto a high shelf.

opening.title: Rolling the Paper Cones
opening.need: 4 sheets of paper or thin card · masking tape · 2 rubber bands.
steps: Roll one sheet into a cone with a wide mouth and a hole at the point big enough for her ear. Hold it closed while she winds the rubber band on.
She rolls the next two herself, one fat and one thin. Crooked is fine, and turns out to be useful.
Hold each one to her ear and say nothing about which sounds best. She finds that out at 9:15.

main.title: The Ear Trumpet Test
materials: 4 sheets of paper or thin card
A ticking clock, or your phone playing something quiet in the next room
1 saucepan and a wooden spoon, for the far-away noise
steps: Send the noise away first. A ticking clock in the next room, or the saucepan and spoon at the far end of the hall.
Bare ears first. Let her tell you how much she gets from where she stands.
Cone one against one ear, other ear covered with her hand. Same sound, same distance. Ask her better or the same.
Cone two, then cone three, in that order, at that distance, with nothing else changed between goes.
She calls the winner, even where you would have picked another. Tape that cone so it holds its shape.
She decorates the winner with crayons and it is hers for the day. The other two go on the shelf until 4:15, and she says what happens to them.
main.tip: Keep the sound the same and change one cone at a time. She is running a fair test without the words for it, and swapping the noise halfway wrecks the hour.

outside.title: The Listening Stop
paras: Walk to a bench or a low wall and stop dead for two minutes. Nobody talks. Hold up a finger for each sound she catches: a car, a crow, a door, a plane, wind in a bare hedge, her own breathing. Early March carries sound further than summer does, with no leaves out yet to soak it up. Take the trumpet and let her aim it at the furthest one.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months and turns his whole head to a sound now instead of moving his eyes and giving up. Sit behind him and shake a set of keys to one side, then the other, and watch the head come round. Once Azlyn has finished testing, hand him the saucepan and the wooden spoon. A pan is the loudest thing in the house and he knows it.

second.title: The String Telephone
second.intro: Two cups and five meters of string between two rooms. She works out the rule before you get to say it.
materials: 2 paper cups or clean yogurt cups
1 pencil or skewer to pierce the cups (adult only)
2 paperclips or matchsticks to anchor the knots
steps: Pierce one small hole in the bottom of each cup yourself, dead center, with her hands well back.
Thread the string in from the outside and knot it round a paperclip inside the cup so it cannot pull back through. She holds the cup while you tie.
Test it across one room, both of you standing, string pulled tight. You talk, she listens, then swap over.

Let the string go slack and try again. She gets nothing, and she will tell you before you ask. Run it round a door frame into the next room and it dies at the corner too. Leave her to find the straight line that brings it back.
Whisper down it. That is the run that convinces her, because she can see your mouth moving and hears nothing without the cup at her ear.
Take it down, wind the string up and put it away before you do anything else.
second.tip: Give her the listening end first. A three-year-old handed the talking end shouts into the cup, and a shout crosses the room through the air anyway.

alternatives: One cup and one length of string, held to the ear like a stethoscope.
Tap a message down the radiator pipe and listen at the other end.
Hide a ticking clock and let her find it by ear alone.
outAgain: The library, and let her ask for the book out loud instead of pointing
The indoor play center if the library is packed with a school group
The park, for the swings on the way back
The thrift store, for a book she gets to keep
days.krestonPM: Take him to the library and put him down in the board-book corner. At 8 months he chews books, which is what board books are for, and he bangs two together before he opens either. New faces at storytime may be too much this month, so sit at the edge with him facing you.

insight.headline: Testing before committing is a habit worth encouraging.
paras: Azlyn made three cones and found out which one worked before any of them got decorated. That order matters more than the cones do. A three-year-old who tries the rough version first is learning that a plan is a thing you check, and the check costs her nothing here, because the materials are paper and tape. Engineers call it prototyping and Azlyn calls it trying it out. You back it up every time you let a poor idea run to its end instead of heading it off, because the cone that heard nothing taught her as much as the one she kept.

days.safety: Take the string telephone down and put the string away the second you finish. A loop of string at toddler height is a strangulation risk, and Kreston crawls now, so it never stays up while you make a cup of tea. Scissors and the skewer stay with you.

days.title: Following Her Nose
days.prepTonight: Fill the six pots after she is in bed, foil and a band over each one with a few holes pierced through, and pare one curl of peel off an orange for the sixth pot.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: Six Pots with Holes in the Lid

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The House That Smells of Oranges

opening.title: Six Pots with Holes in the Lid
opening.need: the six filled pots · masking tape · 1 marker.
steps: Set the six in a row on the table and let her look at them without opening a thing.
Show her how to waft: cupped hand over the top, a pull of air toward her face. Nose down on the foil gets her a lungful of cinnamon.
She lines them up, the one she likes best at one end and the one she likes least at the other. Nothing gets written down yet.

main.title: The Smell Words
materials: 6 small jars or yogurt cups with foil lids
Ground coffee, ground cinnamon, orange peel, a dried herb, a sliver of soap, a drop of vanilla
Masking tape for labels and a marker
steps: Sit opposite her with the six pots on your side of the table and hand them across one at a time.
Ask for a word and stop there. A word for it, not the name of it. Sit through the silence while she looks.
Write her word on a strip of masking tape and stick it on that pot. Her spelling if she has any, your handwriting if she does not.
If she names the thing, take that as her word too. Coffee is a word.
Go round a second time in a different order. Two or three words will change, and both versions go on the tape. Read the six labels back at the end and let her move any pot she wants to.
main.tip: Do not tell her what is in the pots. Naming them ends the sniffing, because she has the answer and no reason to go back.

outside.title: Wet Earth and Woodsmoke
paras: Early March smells of wet ground. Lift a handful of soil from a flower bed, a wet stone, or a dead leaf from under a hedge and hold it up to her. Rain on cold earth releases a smell with a name of its own, petrichor, and she knows it long before she has the word. Then go hunting: a chimney with smoke, trash day, a laundry vent. One word each.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months and knows your smell better than your face on a bad day, which is why your sweater settles him faster than a toy. Hold him in the kitchen doorway once the oranges start and watch his face open up. Hold the third orange yourself, cut side toward him, and let him get his nose into it. Peel breaks off in hard pieces under a gum, so it stays in your hand and never in his.

second.title: The House That Smells of Oranges
second.intro: Peel and cinnamon go on the stovetop at the lowest setting, and the house changes around her while she draws.
materials: 1 cinnamon stick or a spoon of ground cinnamon
This week's written-down words, to read back at the end
steps: Peel two oranges with her. She pulls the pieces off in whatever sizes come away.
Drop the peel into the pan with the cinnamon and enough water to cover it. Back burner, lowest heat, handle turned in.
Set her up at the table beside the kitchen with paper, crayons and paint, and no subject.
Say nothing about the smell. It arrives on its own over about fifteen minutes, and she will be the one who mentions it.
Top the water up as it drops. She can hand you the pitcher.
Halfway through, read her the week's written-down words: the touch words, the taste words, this morning's smell words.
Ask which one she wants to keep. Write that word big across the top of whatever she has drawn, and put it on the fridge.
second.tip: Hold off asking her what she has drawn. If she wants you to know, she tells you, and the question turns her paper into a test she can get wrong.

alternatives: Orange peel and cloves pushed into a pomander, no stovetop involved.
Warm cinnamon toast and eat it while it fills the kitchen.
Bury the six pots in a basket of rice and let her dig them out.
outAgain: The grocery store, and let her pick the fruit by smell before it goes in
The bakery, for the doorway more than the bun
The market, if it runs today
A loop past the pizza place, the florist and the laundromat, naming each one
days.krestonPM: At 8 months he sits up in the cart seat and takes in a store that is loud, bright and full of strangers, so twenty minutes is plenty. Keep him facing you rather than out, and give him something cold from the chiller to hold, too big to fit in his mouth.

insight.headline: She tells you what it is once nobody has asked.
paras: You already describe more of it than you think. You used a lot of red down this side and that line goes all the way to the corner are sentences she can answer, and she answers them. The one that stalls her is what is it?, because she hears a test with one right answer, and half the time she did not set out to make a thing at all. Stay with what her hands did. You pressed hard here and soft here. She picks up the words for it, carries no pressure to have meant anything, and nine times in ten she tells you what it is herself, on her own timing.

days.safety: A pan simmering on the stovetop for an hour with a crawling 8-month-old in the house. Back burner only, handle turned in, and it goes off the heat if you leave the kitchen. Ground cinnamon and coffee sting in the eyes, so the pots stay lidded and go up high when she is done with them.
